compare_blocks.body:

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional example, two relatives get up to help when someone at home feels unwell. Both are available and take responsibility. Their actions tell the family what they did that night, but they cannot establish a type.

The resemblance comes mainly from the shared E: attention and energy turn more often toward what is happening outside, for example by engaging with people and events around them. That describes direction only, not who is warmer or who is better at caring for someone.

The difference sits on three preferences: ESTP more often takes facts and experience first (S), ENFJ more often takes connections and possibilities first (N); ESTP more often judges by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often puts people and values into the judgement (F); dealing with the outside, ENFJ more often settles an arrangement (J) and ESTP more often keeps options open (P).

### The same family night, two kinds of material and two standards

In this fictional scene, an older relative feels unwell during the night. In an emergency, call the local emergency number promptly and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The comparison here concerns how relatives organise and communicate the same information.

After contacting professional help, both relatives have the same information and responsibilities. One question is who needs an update and how the message may affect them. Another is what makes an update useful in every case, such as whether it helps someone take responsibility for an agreed task. Those are different decision criteria. Either relative can also collect and share the confirmed facts, following the instructions they receive.

Each approach has a cost. After contacting professional help, one relative may summarise what is known for the family, while another records precise observations for staff. The same person can do both. Do not delay seeking help to complete a record. The cost is not about preference but about who was present and who owns outward communication that night.

Order is not the criterion. Either relative can contact help promptly and share the information already available. Who takes on each communication task depends on who is present, what they know and any professional guidance. Role, duty, experience and the conditions of the night all rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

To practise the distinction you do not need an emergency. Take a household matter that is not urgent — whether to fit grab rails in the relative's home, who collects the children at the weekend — and watch what each person more often asks: "who is affected by this, who will worry", or "which items are confirmed and which are still missing". Use the exercise to reflect on communication in an ordinary setting without making medical decisions.

### Why the four function names match and the order shifts by two

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. All four names match, and the positions rotate by two: ENFJ's dominant Fe is ESTP's third, ENFJ's inferior Ti is ESTP's auxiliary; conversely ESTP's dominant Se is ENFJ's third, and ESTP's inferior Ni is ENFJ's auxiliary. This is a cyclic shift, not a reversal.

The three preference letters have to be read separately. S/N is about sourcing: trusting comparable facts and experience more, or noticing connections and possibilities faster. T/F is about the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what the matter means for the people involved. J/P is about the outward stance: settling arrangements and conclusions first, or keeping options until new information arrives. The three cannot substitute for one another, and none can be decided by speed, sequence of actions or improvised adjustment.

The two share one perceiving axis, Se–Ni, and one judging axis, Fe–Ti; ENFJ is described as leading with a judging process (Fe), and ESTP with a perceiving process (Se). Those are dominant positions in the model. They do not establish what either person will do first.

Whether the third position is labelled inward or outward is not consistent across published tables: for ENFJ's Se and ESTP's Fe, some tables give only the function name without settling the attitude. When you meet a different version, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not change the first two and does not explain how early someone moves. Both base pages are the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: what follows is a fictional night at home and a review at the breakfast table the next morning. It concerns communication and the organisation of information only, not reading signs, deciding whether someone can be moved, or any medication decision. In an emergency, seek help first: call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or the on-site clinician's instructions; record information afterwards if there is capacity to spare.

When two people work together, friction usually appears when one is still on the phone and the other already has shoes on. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which category of information each handled first.

### Two in the morning: both are organising information

(Fictional scene.) That night, both can do the same thing: write down what is already known — when the discomfort started, what medicine was taken, what the relative said. Either can write it; only the category that comes to mind first differs.

In this fictional scene, both relatives separate confirmed facts from guesses. Then they can ask two different questions about the same update: what information matters to the people affected, and what consistent criteria should guide what they share? Either person can use both questions. The order depends on the task, responsibilities and information.

The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type. Whether to give medication, whether to go to emergency care and which department are decisions for the treating clinician or the emergency crew; the household's job is to bring the observed facts and the medication record. Replacing "I judged it was fine" with "this is what I saw" removes half the argument.

### "Should we have gone last night?" at the breakfast table

(Fictional scene.) At breakfast the next morning, the family reviews what happened. A sister-in-law says "wasn't last night too much fuss", and a brother adds "we could have waited".

In this fictional breakfast discussion, either person can explain the verified sequence of events and acknowledge how frightening it was for the relative. For a fair review, the family can ask whether they applied the same communication rules to each person and whether the way they shared updates met the needs of people directly affected.

The discussion can turn into blame if the family mixes up how the night felt and which tasks were agreed. The sister-in-law wants "not this much disruption next time"; the brother wants "under what conditions we must go". Both can be answered at once, but someone has to separate them.

Who says which sentence first is not a criterion. ESTP will also pour the relative a glass of water before explaining, and ENFJ will also turn the timeline into one message for the clinician; fatigue, who usually runs the household and who was present all rewrite the order.

As for "under what conditions we must go", that belongs to the clinician or the emergency guidance. The household records the facts and the decision taken, and does not invent a threshold of signs to pin by the door.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is "ENFJ is better at caring". Caring is a skill, and practice and experience account for much of it; ESTP can also steady an older person and speak warmly, only they more often handle the few facts in the room first rather than how the people present feel.

The second is "ESTP is bolder". Whether someone will go out at night depends on the roads, the medical history, past experience and whether anyone else could go; treating decisiveness as a personality label misses that ENFJ is equally brisk once it is clear what has to be done.

The third comes from "three letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four function names, in a different order under the convention used here; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody at two in the morning, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who called first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different nights; sequence carries no classificatory value.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: In a fictional example, two relatives get up to help when someone at home feels unwell. Both are available and take responsibility. Their actions tell the family what they did that night, but they cannot establish a type.

The resemblance comes mainly from the shared E: attention and energy turn more often toward what is happening outside, for example by engaging with people and events around them. That describes direction only, not who is warmer or who is better at caring for someone.

The difference sits on three preferences: ESTP more often takes facts and experience first (S), ENFJ more often takes connections and possibilities first (N); ESTP more often judges by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often puts people and values into the judgement (F); dealing with the outside, ENFJ more often settles an arrangement (J) and ESTP more often keeps options open (P).
### The same family night, two kinds of material and two standards

In this fictional scene, an older relative feels unwell during the night. In an emergency, call the local emergency number promptly and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The comparison here concerns how relatives organise and communicate the same information.

After contacting professional help, both relatives have the same information and responsibilities. One question is who needs an update and how the message may affect them. Another is what makes an update useful in every case, such as whether it helps someone take responsibility for an agreed task. Those are different decision criteria. Either relative can also collect and share the confirmed facts, following the instructions they receive.

Each approach has a cost. After contacting professional help, one relative may summarise what is known for the family, while another records precise observations for staff. The same person can do both. Do not delay seeking help to complete a record. The cost is not about preference but about who was present and who owns outward communication that night.

Order is not the criterion. Either relative can contact help promptly and share the information already available. Who takes on each communication task depends on who is present, what they know and any professional guidance. Role, duty, experience and the conditions of the night all rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

To practise the distinction you do not need an emergency. Take a household matter that is not urgent — whether to fit grab rails in the relative's home, who collects the children at the weekend — and watch what each person more often asks: "who is affected by this, who will worry", or "which items are confirmed and which are still missing". Use the exercise to reflect on communication in an ordinary setting without making medical decisions.
### Why the four function names match and the order shifts by two

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. All four names match, and the positions rotate by two: ENFJ's dominant Fe is ESTP's third, ENFJ's inferior Ti is ESTP's auxiliary; conversely ESTP's dominant Se is ENFJ's third, and ESTP's inferior Ni is ENFJ's auxiliary. This is a cyclic shift, not a reversal.

The three preference letters have to be read separately. S/N is about sourcing: trusting comparable facts and experience more, or noticing connections and possibilities faster. T/F is about the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what the matter means for the people involved. J/P is about the outward stance: settling arrangements and conclusions first, or keeping options until new information arrives. The three cannot substitute for one another, and none can be decided by speed, sequence of actions or improvised adjustment.

The two share one perceiving axis, Se–Ni, and one judging axis, Fe–Ti; ENFJ is described as leading with a judging process (Fe), and ESTP with a perceiving process (Se). Those are dominant positions in the model. They do not establish what either person will do first.

Whether the third position is labelled inward or outward is not consistent across published tables: for ENFJ's Se and ESTP's Fe, some tables give only the function name without settling the attitude. When you meet a different version, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not change the first two and does not explain how early someone moves. Both base pages are the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).

body: The premise for the table is aligned conditions: the same night, the same older relative, the same information, the same transport and access to care. If only one person is the main carer, their responsibilities and access to information may explain the difference.
Both relatives can use any of the approaches below. The table covers communication and household coordination after help is reached. It does not set criteria for when to seek care.

| Same fictional night, relative, information and responsibilities | ENFJ: the basis more likely attended to | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to wake another family member | Weigh the family member’s needs and how being contacted would affect them | Apply the same criterion to each option, such as whether an essential task is still unassigned | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| What medicines are in the house and when they were last used | How these details string into one account that can be stated clearly | Names, expiry dates and the time of the last dose, checked item by item | Names, dates and records are checked by both; how information is presented follows the listener |
| After contacting professional help, agree who will update the family | Agree on a temporary point of contact and revise it if needed | Keep several ways of sharing the update open as circumstances change | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both choose what to share from the same confirmed family update | Weigh which confirmed details matter most to those affected | Apply a consistent rule to choose relevant details, such as whether they affect who can help | T/F: different criteria for the same choice. Both share confirmed information only; clinical questions go to professionals. |
| "Was last night too much fuss?" at breakfast | Weigh how the same verified events affected the relative and others | Weigh those events against a consistent standard for reviewing the family’s coordination | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Whether to take today off | Settle tomorrow's arrangement and who covers the shift | Keep coverage options open while confirming who can take the shift | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ENFJ who has worked ten years of night shifts more often collects information by professional habit, and an ESTP facing this for the first time may simply stand by the bed. The same person also changes approach with the information they hold, their caring duty and whether anyone has already reached support, so these rows cannot be used to classify.

body: Scope note: what follows is a fictional night at home and a review at the breakfast table the next morning. It concerns communication and the organisation of information only, not reading signs, deciding whether someone can be moved, or any medication decision. In an emergency, seek help first: call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or the on-site clinician's instructions; record information afterwards if there is capacity to spare.

When two people work together, friction usually appears when one is still on the phone and the other already has shoes on. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which category of information each handled first.
### Two in the morning: both are organising information

(Fictional scene.) That night, both can do the same thing: write down what is already known — when the discomfort started, what medicine was taken, what the relative said. Either can write it; only the category that comes to mind first differs.

In this fictional scene, both relatives separate confirmed facts from guesses. Then they can ask two different questions about the same update: what information matters to the people affected, and what consistent criteria should guide what they share? Either person can use both questions. The order depends on the task, responsibilities and information.

The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type. Whether to give medication, whether to go to emergency care and which department are decisions for the treating clinician or the emergency crew; the household's job is to bring the observed facts and the medication record. Replacing "I judged it was fine" with "this is what I saw" removes half the argument.
### "Should we have gone last night?" at the breakfast table
(Fictional scene.) At breakfast the next morning, the family reviews what happened. A sister-in-law says "wasn't last night too much fuss", and a brother adds "we could have waited".

In this fictional breakfast discussion, either person can explain the verified sequence of events and acknowledge how frightening it was for the relative. For a fair review, the family can ask whether they applied the same communication rules to each person and whether the way they shared updates met the needs of people directly affected.

The discussion can turn into blame if the family mixes up how the night felt and which tasks were agreed. The sister-in-law wants "not this much disruption next time"; the brother wants "under what conditions we must go". Both can be answered at once, but someone has to separate them.

Who says which sentence first is not a criterion. ESTP will also pour the relative a glass of water before explaining, and ENFJ will also turn the timeline into one message for the clinician; fatigue, who usually runs the household and who was present all rewrite the order.

As for "under what conditions we must go", that belongs to the clinician or the emergency guidance. The household records the facts and the decision taken, and does not invent a threshold of signs to pin by the door.

body: The first misread is "ENFJ is better at caring". Caring is a skill, and practice and experience account for much of it; ESTP can also steady an older person and speak warmly, only they more often handle the few facts in the room first rather than how the people present feel.

The second is "ESTP is bolder". Whether someone will go out at night depends on the roads, the medical history, past experience and whether anyone else could go; treating decisiveness as a personality label misses that ENFJ is equally brisk once it is clear what has to be done.

The third comes from "three letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four function names, in a different order under the convention used here; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody at two in the morning, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who called first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different nights; sequence carries no classificatory value.
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP: avoiding misreads

body: When earlier and later results differ, check the item bank, language version, scoring convention and what you were referring to when you answered, rather than reasoning backwards from the result to "I must have acted first". A role that rewards keeping people informed or responding quickly may affect how you answer. Note which setting you had in mind and which decisions you had the freedom to make.

Put the practice in everyday scenes that are not emergencies and where the roles are similar: pick a few recent household matters — whether to fit grab rails, how to arrange weekend pick-ups, whether to replace an old appliance — and write a few lines for each: which information you trusted, which standard you weighed it against, and whether you settled the arrangement or kept options open. If "whether the standard is consistent", "what it means for the people involved" and "settle it or look again" recur, that is worth discussing as your habit in sourcing and judging.

Counterexamples matter as much: if you used the other kind of evidence on the same matter, both approaches are within your range. These notes are for reflection, are not scored, do not assign a type, and a few weeks of trend cannot replace an interpretation of an assessment result.

- S/N: the ESTP side, S (Sensing), more often takes observable facts and past experience first; the ENFJ side, N (Intuition), more often takes connections, patterns and possibilities first.
- T/F: the ESTP side, T (Thinking), more often judges by impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently; the ENFJ side, F (Feeling), more often puts people and values into the judgement.
- J/P: the ENFJ side, J (Judging), more often settles outer arrangements and conclusions first; the ESTP side, P (Perceiving), more often keeps options open and adjusts to new information.

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Fe–Ni–Se–Ti for ENFJ and Se–Ti–Fe–Ni for ESTP. All four names are shared, with dominant and third swapped and auxiliary and inferior swapped; the attitude of the third process (Se for ENFJ, Fe for ESTP) is labelled differently elsewhere, and this writing is a convention adopted here rather than the Foundation's only version.

These preferences describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict the order of behaviour, who acts first, or whether two people work well together. In the same family situation both types may make the call first, recheck first or comfort first; order is shaped more by role, duty, experience and conditions on the night.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional example, two relatives get up to help when someone at home feels unwell. Both are available and take responsibility. Their actions tell the family what they did that night, but they cannot establish a type.

The resemblance comes mainly from the shared E: attention and energy turn more often toward what is happening outside, for example by engaging with people and events around them. That describes direction only, not who is warmer or who is better at caring for someone.

The difference sits on three preferences: ESTP more often takes facts and experience first (S), ENFJ more often takes connections and possibilities first (N); ESTP more often judges by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often puts people and values into the judgement (F); dealing with the outside, ENFJ more often settles an arrangement (J) and ESTP more often keeps options open (P).

### The same family night, two kinds of material and two standards

In this fictional scene, an older relative feels unwell during the night. In an emergency, call the local emergency number promptly and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The comparison here concerns how relatives organise and communicate the same information.

After contacting professional help, both relatives have the same information and responsibilities. One question is who needs an update and how the message may affect them. Another is what makes an update useful in every case, such as whether it helps someone take responsibility for an agreed task. Those are different decision criteria. Either relative can also collect and share the confirmed facts, following the instructions they receive.

Each approach has a cost. After contacting professional help, one relative may summarise what is known for the family, while another records precise observations for staff. The same person can do both. Do not delay seeking help to complete a record. The cost is not about preference but about who was present and who owns outward communication that night.

Order is not the criterion. Either relative can contact help promptly and share the information already available. Who takes on each communication task depends on who is present, what they know and any professional guidance. Role, duty, experience and the conditions of the night all rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

To practise the distinction you do not need an emergency. Take a household matter that is not urgent — whether to fit grab rails in the relative's home, who collects the children at the weekend — and watch what each person more often asks: "who is affected by this, who will worry", or "which items are confirmed and which are still missing". Use the exercise to reflect on communication in an ordinary setting without making medical decisions.

### Why the four function names match and the order shifts by two

In the common four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. All four names match, and the positions rotate by two: ENFJ's dominant Fe is ESTP's third, ENFJ's inferior Ti is ESTP's auxiliary; conversely ESTP's dominant Se is ENFJ's third, and ESTP's inferior Ni is ENFJ's auxiliary. This is a cyclic shift, not a reversal.

The three preference letters have to be read separately. S/N is about sourcing: trusting comparable facts and experience more, or noticing connections and possibilities faster. T/F is about the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what the matter means for the people involved. J/P is about the outward stance: settling arrangements and conclusions first, or keeping options until new information arrives. The three cannot substitute for one another, and none can be decided by speed, sequence of actions or improvised adjustment.

The two share one perceiving axis, Se–Ni, and one judging axis, Fe–Ti; ENFJ is described as leading with a judging process (Fe), and ESTP with a perceiving process (Se). Those are dominant positions in the model. They do not establish what either person will do first.

Whether the third position is labelled inward or outward is not consistent across published tables: for ENFJ's Se and ESTP's Fe, some tables give only the function name without settling the attitude. When you meet a different version, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not change the first two and does not explain how early someone moves. Both base pages are the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP: shared ground and the core difference

sections.body_md:
The premise for the table is aligned conditions: the same night, the same older relative, the same information, the same transport and access to care. If only one person is the main carer, their responsibilities and access to information may explain the difference.

Both relatives can use any of the approaches below. The table covers communication and household coordination after help is reached. It does not set criteria for when to seek care.

| Same fictional night, relative, information and responsibilities | ENFJ: the basis more likely attended to | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to wake another family member | Weigh the family member’s needs and how being contacted would affect them | Apply the same criterion to each option, such as whether an essential task is still unassigned | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| What medicines are in the house and when they were last used | How these details string into one account that can be stated clearly | Names, expiry dates and the time of the last dose, checked item by item | Names, dates and records are checked by both; how information is presented follows the listener |
| After contacting professional help, agree who will update the family | Agree on a temporary point of contact and revise it if needed | Keep several ways of sharing the update open as circumstances change | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both choose what to share from the same confirmed family update | Weigh which confirmed details matter most to those affected | Apply a consistent rule to choose relevant details, such as whether they affect who can help | T/F: different criteria for the same choice. Both share confirmed information only; clinical questions go to professionals. |
| "Was last night too much fuss?" at breakfast | Weigh how the same verified events affected the relative and others | Weigh those events against a consistent standard for reviewing the family’s coordination | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Whether to take today off | Settle tomorrow's arrangement and who covers the shift | Keep coverage options open while confirming who can take the shift | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ENFJ who has worked ten years of night shifts more often collects information by professional habit, and an ESTP facing this for the first time may simply stand by the bed. The same person also changes approach with the information they hold, their caring duty and whether anyone has already reached support, so these rows cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: what follows is a fictional night at home and a review at the breakfast table the next morning. It concerns communication and the organisation of information only, not reading signs, deciding whether someone can be moved, or any medication decision. In an emergency, seek help first: call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or the on-site clinician's instructions; record information afterwards if there is capacity to spare.

When two people work together, friction usually appears when one is still on the phone and the other already has shoes on. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which category of information each handled first.

### Two in the morning: both are organising information

(Fictional scene.) That night, both can do the same thing: write down what is already known — when the discomfort started, what medicine was taken, what the relative said. Either can write it; only the category that comes to mind first differs.

In this fictional scene, both relatives separate confirmed facts from guesses. Then they can ask two different questions about the same update: what information matters to the people affected, and what consistent criteria should guide what they share? Either person can use both questions. The order depends on the task, responsibilities and information.

The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type. Whether to give medication, whether to go to emergency care and which department are decisions for the treating clinician or the emergency crew; the household's job is to bring the observed facts and the medication record. Replacing "I judged it was fine" with "this is what I saw" removes half the argument.

### "Should we have gone last night?" at the breakfast table

(Fictional scene.) At breakfast the next morning, the family reviews what happened. A sister-in-law says "wasn't last night too much fuss", and a brother adds "we could have waited".

In this fictional breakfast discussion, either person can explain the verified sequence of events and acknowledge how frightening it was for the relative. For a fair review, the family can ask whether they applied the same communication rules to each person and whether the way they shared updates met the needs of people directly affected.

The discussion can turn into blame if the family mixes up how the night felt and which tasks were agreed. The sister-in-law wants "not this much disruption next time"; the brother wants "under what conditions we must go". Both can be answered at once, but someone has to separate them.

Who says which sentence first is not a criterion. ESTP will also pour the relative a glass of water before explaining, and ENFJ will also turn the timeline into one message for the clinician; fatigue, who usually runs the household and who was present all rewrite the order.

As for "under what conditions we must go", that belongs to the clinician or the emergency guidance. The household records the facts and the decision taken, and does not invent a threshold of signs to pin by the door.
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP: care at home and the next morning

sections.body_md:
The first misread is "ENFJ is better at caring". Caring is a skill, and practice and experience account for much of it; ESTP can also steady an older person and speak warmly, only they more often handle the few facts in the room first rather than how the people present feel.

The second is "ESTP is bolder". Whether someone will go out at night depends on the roads, the medical history, past experience and whether anyone else could go; treating decisiveness as a personality label misses that ENFJ is equally brisk once it is clear what has to be done.

The third comes from "three letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four function names, in a different order under the convention used here; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody at two in the morning, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who called first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different nights; sequence carries no classificatory value.
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When earlier and later results differ, check the item bank, language version, scoring convention and what you were referring to when you answered, rather than reasoning backwards from the result to "I must have acted first". A role that rewards keeping people informed or responding quickly may affect how you answer. Note which setting you had in mind and which decisions you had the freedom to make.

Put the practice in everyday scenes that are not emergencies and where the roles are similar: pick a few recent household matters — whether to fit grab rails, how to arrange weekend pick-ups, whether to replace an old appliance — and write a few lines for each: which information you trusted, which standard you weighed it against, and whether you settled the arrangement or kept options open. If "whether the standard is consistent", "what it means for the people involved" and "settle it or look again" recur, that is worth discussing as your habit in sourcing and judging.

Counterexamples matter as much: if you used the other kind of evidence on the same matter, both approaches are within your range. These notes are for reflection, are not scored, do not assign a type, and a few weeks of trend cannot replace an interpretation of an assessment result.
sections.title: ENFJ and ESTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
S/N, T/F and J/P; only E is shared.

S/N compares sourcing: trusting comparable facts and experience, or noticing connections and possibilities faster; T/F compares the basis for judgement: impersonal consistency, or people and values; J/P compares the outward stance: forming an arrangement first, or keeping options first. All three have to be read separately. Both types may call first, gather information first or comfort first in the same event, and sequence is not a criterion; what discriminates better is which kind of evidence is cited more often across several comparable situations.
items.question: What exactly are the three differences between ENFJ and ESTP?

items.answer:
Because the positions rotate rather than reverse: Fe moves from dominant to third, Ti from inferior to auxiliary, Se from third to dominant, and Ni from auxiliary to inferior.

Both types have the same four function labels in this convention, with different dominant and auxiliary positions. But positions describe emphasis in preference only; they do not predict the order of behaviour, whether two people work well together or who attracts whom — those depend far more on the specific people, their duties and their shared experience.
items.question: The four function names are the same, so why do they read as opposites?

items.answer:
Yes, but not by sequence and not by which feels more natural.

What discriminates better is the reason: across several comparable situations, do you more often cite "the confirmed facts and a standard that can be applied consistently", or "what this means for the people involved and who should be included"? One person uses both reasons; the difference is which is taken up first more often. A single behaviour, one phrasing or the order on one night cannot type anyone; experience and duty can push performance to the other side, which is training and ability, not a change of preference.
items.question: ESTP also comforts people first and ENFJ also acts immediately — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Do not divide by type. In an emergency, seek help first: call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or the on-site clinician's instructions; record information afterwards if there is capacity, such as when it was noticed, what medicine was taken and who has already been contacted.

Either relative can contact emergency services promptly and report what is already known. Who records information or updates the family afterwards depends on who is available and what the dispatcher or clinician advises. Confirming signs, deciding whether someone can be moved and deciding on medication are medical and emergency judgements, and belong to professionals or the dispatcher.
items.question: Something happens at night — who should do what?

items.answer:
In the fictional scene, the family may disagree about how they coordinated. One person worries that the response caused unnecessary disruption, while another wonders whether the family communicated quickly enough.

The way out is to separate two conversations. On feeling, acknowledge that everyone was frightened that night and nobody was trying to cause trouble; on process, record only the facts and the decision taken, and take the question of when medical care is required to the clinician or the emergency guidance rather than agreeing a threshold of signs at home. Writing it down by the door is fine, as long as what is written is contacts and the care record, not a self-made criterion.
items.question: Where do families with ENFJ and ESTP most often get stuck?

items.answer:
Check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then which kind of experience you were referring to when you answered: projects at work, or situations in family care. Circumstances push answers toward one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at which of S/N, T/F and J/P sit closer to the boundary; sitting near a boundary only means that label is sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two complete types both hold. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer that you are on a boundary, and no retest interval is prescribed.

The arrangement of the four positions on this page, especially the attitude of the third process, is the common writing adopted here and is an editorial convention; sources handle it differently, and this writing is not presented as the Foundation's only version. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, screening candidates or predicting relationships; medical and emergency judgements belong to qualified professionals and emergency dispatchers.
